widgets_values:
Exercise: refining a stereo point cloud with a SECOND stereo pair

Read the top level left to right; every box is a subgraph (double-click
to open one). Two pairs of the same street (frames 000000 and 000001)
are reconstructed separately, then registered and merged.

'Stereo Pair To Cloud' (one instance per pair)
  Calibration from CSV - K from the per-image vertical FOV, R and T from
  the CSV columns. The two frames have DIFFERENT intrinsics (vfov 1.015
  vs 0.758 rad, f 431 vs 602 px), so each instance calibrates and
  rectifies on its own; most of the apparent 'moved forward' between the
  two images is that zoom, not motion. Then stereoRectify +
  initUndistortRectifyMap + remap (BORDER_CONSTANT), disparity, and
  reprojectImageTo3D.

  DISPARITY, AND THE TRAP IN IT. 'CV Stereo Disparity (WLS filtered)'
  runs SGBM in both directions and left-right-checks them, which is
  what produces the confidence map - and the confidence map is the
  only thing taken from it here. Its FILLED disparity is not used:
  the WLS prior is fronto-parallel, so it bends the textureless
  slanted road into a ridge. Measured on this pair, a plane fit
  through the road band goes from 0.06 m RMS / 98% inliers (raw SGBM)
  to 0.36 m / 33%, and 0.34 m of that is on pixels SGBM ALREADY had
  right - it corrupts good data, it does not only fill badly. Lambda
  just trades that against coverage (100 -> 0.09 m but 70% valid).
  So the RAW map is handed to 'CV Disparity Interpolate (Edge-Aware)'
  with the confidence map as a seed gate. RIC fits a local PLANE per
  superpixel - which is what a road is - so the road survives (0.06 m
  RMS / 97% inliers) at ~100% coverage, with 85-90% of its disparity
  edges landing on image edges. The other way round (cv2.inpaint) keeps the road and
  smears every silhouette: 15% by that same measure.

  AND THEN THE SKY. Making the disparity dense also fills the sky,
  and those points are not catchable downstream: they land at a
  median 18 m, inside the range filter, and were 26% (A) / 30% (B)
  of each cloud. The nested 'Sky Mask' subgraph builds a
  mask and 'CV Filter Points 3D By Mask' drops those points (it
  filters the colours in lockstep). Two near-misses:
  * the WLS confidence is HIGHER in the sky (207) than on real
    content (163) - a uniform region returns the same wrong match in
    both directions, so the left-right check is satisfied;
  * gating the sky out of the interpolator's SEEDS makes it WORSE
    (25.7% -> 31.7% sky points), because RIC then extrapolates the
    neighbouring planes over the whole region unopposed. The mask
    must be applied to the POINTS.
  THE MASK IS A HEURISTIC TUNED TO THIS DATASET: 'flat
  (|Laplacian| < 2), opened, and connected to the TOP image edge'.
  That fits CARLA - cloudless, overexposed, noise-free, camera
  level. Expect it to fail on textured clouds, a noisy real sensor,
  sun glare, a downward-looking camera or indoors. For real footage
  use a semantic segmentation ONNX with a sky class (Cityscapes /
  ADE20K) through the existing 'DNN Forward All' -> 'Pick Output'
  -> 'Seg Masks' pipeline: a model file, no new nodes.
  Inside the subgraph, three choices are load-bearing:
  * the OPEN before the connectivity test. Without it the flat
    region leaks through the gaps between leaves, the component
    test follows the leak, and the mask swallows the tree and the
    facade behind it - at |Laplacian| < 3 it takes 70% of frame B,
    road included. With the opening the same threshold gives 21%.
  * 'Keep Largest Component' would pick the ROAD (also flat, and
    larger than any single sky component), and 'Select Component At
    Point' would catch one of the 18 pieces the lamp post cuts the
    sky into. Reaching the TOP edge is the actual predicate.
  * the border margin is 4 px and it has to be. cv2.remap with
    BORDER_CONSTANT leaves a DARK SEAM one row deep at the top of a
    rectified frame, and the Gaussian + Laplacian smear it over
    three more rows, so the flat mask only starts answering at row
    4. At margin 2 the sky right of the lamp post in pair B is
    never seen and half of B's sky stayed in the cloud. Not the
    opening - OpenCV pads erosion with +inf, so morphology never
    shrinks a region at the image border.
  COLOUR SAMPLING WAS TRIED AND IS WORSE. Flood-filling from the top
  row with a sampled sky colour (cv2.floodFill, fixed range) reaches
  100% of the sky and also swallows tree tops, a building corner and
  the distant facades - in this washed-out scene everything far away
  is nearly the sky's colour. It masks 18-36% of the hand-labelled
  CONTENT boxes and 4-10% of its masked pixels are strongly
  textured; the shipped mask scores 0.0% on both. The failure mode
  is not the road (mid-ground objects stop the flood first), it is
  the haze at distance. Texture plus connectivity separates those,
  colour does not.

'Match Views (3D Matches)'
  Detects and matches features between the two RECTIFIED LEFT views, then
  'CV Sample Array At Points' reads each match's 3D position out of both
  XYZ maps. The two samplers are CHAINED through valid_in, so 'usable'
  means the depth is valid in BOTH views without a cv2.bitwise_and -
  which returns None on an empty match set and would crash the graph.

'Camera Pose From 3D Matches (PnP)'
  The pose comes from 2D-3D PnP + RANSAC: cloud A's 3D points seen at the
  matched PIXELS of view B. Far better conditioned than fitting 3D to 3D
  - measured on these images, PnP keeps ~135 of ~189 correspondences at
  1.0 px, while the 3D-3D fit (shown alongside for comparison) keeps only
  ~25. Reason: stereo depth noise here is metres (at 28 m one pixel of
  disparity error is ~6 m), and a 3D-3D fit eats that noise twice.
  COORDINATE TRAP: this reconstruction's XYZ is the NEGATION of the usual
  camera frame (Q's last row is negative - that is what the Flip X at the
  end compensates). Projecting -p with P1's K reproduces the source pixel
  EXACTLY (0.00 px), projecting +p is off by hundreds of pixels. So the
  points are negated on the way into PnP, and 'Align Cloud To Reference
  View' negates -> applies the inverse pose -> negates back.

RANGE: each cloud keeps 1..30 m, not 1..60. Depth error grows with Z
squared - f*baseline is 117 px*m, so one 1/16-px disparity step is
0.05 m at 10 m, 0.48 m at 30 m and 1.34 m at 50 m. Past ~30 m a point
cannot be better than half a metre whatever the matcher does. Measured
by projecting cloud A into view B and comparing colours, the cut drops
11% of the points and takes agreement from 74% to 77%. It also shrinks
what the second pair adds, since most of the NEW coverage was far away.
Both limits are PRIMITIVE nodes at the top level, promoted out of the
subgraphs, and ONE pair of them drives all four 'CV Filter Point Cloud'
instances - the two pair clouds and the two ICP downsamples - so the
measurement branch always sees the cloud you are looking at. Turn the
far one while watching the viewer; the coverage-against-trust trade is
a judgement call, not a constant.

'Merge New Coverage'
  'CV Point Cloud Nearest Distance' splits cloud B: points close to an A
  point are duplicates of the overlap and are dropped; the rest is new
  coverage (~38 k points, +21% at the 30 m limit) and is merged in.
  Flip X -> PLY -> viewer at the top level.

OPTIONAL, AND SHIPPED SWITCHED OFF: 'photoconsistency filter'.
A second view is a free quality check - project a point of cloud A
into camera B and compare the colour it carries with the colour that
is actually there; a point at the wrong depth lands somewhere else and
the two disagree. With this graph's own PnP pose (1.09 px), 55% of
cloud A falls inside view B's narrower frame at all, 95% of those
agree within 25 levels, and the filter would drop ~2.2% of the cloud.
It is OFF because it is not free of side effects: a point that is
legitimately OCCLUDED in view B disagrees too, and would be dropped
even though its geometry is fine. Flip the 'Use the photoconsistency
filter?' boolean to true to enable it. The gate is a 'Basic data
handling: IfElse' whose inputs are LAZY, so while it reads false the
branch is not executed at all - it costs nothing to leave wired.
Points that fall outside view B cannot be judged and are KEPT.

HONEST METRICS. Nearest-neighbour distance is a COVERAGE test, not an
alignment score: these clouds are dense near the camera and sparse far
away, so ANY transform that slides the cloud toward the dense near field
lowers the median. Measured here, the unaligned clouds already score
0.30 m and every fitted transform scores worse - that is the metric's
density bias, not evidence about the pose. Judge the pose by PnP's
reprojection error and inlier count instead.

'ICP Measurement' is a MEASUREMENT, not the shipped path:
cv2.ppf_match_3d.ICP is started from the already-good PnP alignment and
its OUTCOME is not predictable. Over ~30 runs it invented anywhere from
0.8 to 16 degrees of rotation and left the nearest-neighbour median
anywhere from unchanged to SEVEN TIMES worse (0.21 -> 1.45 m); twice it
landed 3-13% better. The residual meanwhile only ever lands in one of
two uninformative regimes: ~1e-4 (8.6e-5 to 4.2e-4 measured) whatever
the pose did, or cv2's no-match sentinel near 1e10. That is the lesson
- a residual that small next to a result that unstable is not a
quality measure at all.
This branch is also the one part of the graph that does not reproduce
run to run: ICP samples, and RIC upstream is non-deterministic too, so
expect these numbers to move a little between runs.

Dataset: StereoGeo-CARLA (CC BY 4.0, HuggingFace), 640x480 driving scenes.
